raw_text:
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is a mechanical strategy for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation (AF) based on the observation that, in non-valvular AF, most atrial thrombi arise in the left atrial appendage (LAA) [1]. The procedure aims to exclude the LAA from systemic circulation while avoiding the cumulative bleeding burden and adherence limitations of lifelong oral anticoagulation (OAC). Contemporary LAAC is performed by femoral venous access, transseptal puncture, heparinization, angiographic and echocardiographic sizing, deployment of an endocardial occluder, and confirmation of device stability, seal, and absence of complications.

Early feasibility evolved from PLAATO and first-in-human WATCHMAN experience [2,3]. The pivotal randomized PROTECT AF trial compared WATCHMAN with warfarin and established non-inferiority for a composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular or unexplained death, albeit with an early procedural safety signal [4]. Subsequent analyses showed improved operator safety, durable efficacy, and reductions in hemorrhagic stroke and mortality signals compared with warfarin [5-7]. PREVAIL, designed partly to address PROTECT AF safety concerns, demonstrated improved procedural safety and non-inferiority for late ischemic stroke/systemic embolism, though not for all co-primary efficacy endpoints [8]. Pooled 5-year data from PROTECT AF and PREVAIL supported comparable protection from ischemic events with less hemorrhagic stroke and major non-procedural bleeding after LAAC [9].

The evidence base then shifted from warfarin comparators to direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs). PRAGUE-17 enrolled high-risk patients and found LAAC non-inferior to DOAC therapy for a composite of cardioembolic, cardiovascular, bleeding, and procedural/device outcomes, with maintained results at 4 years and less non-procedural bleeding over time [10,11]. In 2026, CHAMPION-AF broadened the question to anticoagulation-eligible patients and found WATCHMAN FLX–based LAAC non-inferior to DOACs for cardiovascular death, stroke, or systemic embolism and superior for non-procedural bleeding at 3 years [12]. In contrast, CLOSURE-AF, conducted in a high-stroke/high-bleeding-risk population, did not show non-inferiority of LAAC compared with physician-directed best medical therapy, emphasizing that results depend on patient selection, comparator quality, and procedural risk [13].

Device technology has also diversified. The AMPLATZER Amulet uses a lobe-and-disc design intended to provide proximal sealing. In the Amulet IDE randomized trial, Amulet was non-inferior to WATCHMAN 2.5 for safety and effectiveness and superior for complete occlusion, but early procedure-related complications were more frequent, particularly early in operator experience [14]. SWISS-APERO compared Amulet with WATCHMAN/FLX and highlighted trade-offs between sealing, device-related thrombus, and procedure-related findings on systematic imaging [15]. Large Amulet observational studies and WATCHMAN FLX studies show high implant success with improving safety in contemporary practice [16-18].

Real-world registries are central because LAAC recipients are often older and have more prior bleeding than trial populations. The US NCDR LAAO Registry documented high implant success and acceptable in-hospital safety during national adoption [19], and 1-year registry follow-up showed low ischemic stroke rates but substantial mortality and bleeding reflecting baseline comorbidity [20]. EWOLUTION and other registries similarly support feasibility in patients unsuitable for long-term OAC, including those discharged on antiplatelet-only regimens [21,22]. Nevertheless, observational data are vulnerable to selection bias and should complement, not replace, randomized evidence.

The major unresolved issues are patient selection and post-implant antithrombotic therapy. Current guidelines generally support percutaneous LAAC for patients with AF, elevated stroke risk, and a contraindication to long-term OAC, and consider it in selected patients with high bleeding risk or strong preference after shared decision-making [23,24]. Post-procedure therapy varies widely—warfarin plus aspirin, DOAC-based regimens, dual antiplatelet therapy, or abbreviated strategies—because endothelialization must be balanced against bleeding risk [25,26]. Device-related thrombus occurs in a minority but is associated with increased ischemic events [27,28]. Peridevice leak is common; large registry analyses suggest even small leaks may carry incremental thromboembolic risk, supporting meticulous implantation and structured follow-up imaging [29]. Pericardial effusion, device embolization, vascular complications, and procedure-related stroke remain uncommon but important complications, reinforcing the value of operator experience, imaging expertise, and institutional quality programs [30].

In summary, percutaneous LAAC has matured from an alternative for OAC-ineligible patients to a broader stroke-prevention option with randomized evidence against warfarin and selected DOAC-treated populations. Its optimal role is not “instead of anticoagulation” for all AF patients, but as a tailored intervention for those in whom long-term anticoagulation is unsafe, unacceptable, or—based on emerging data—less attractive than a one-time device strategy after careful assessment of procedural risk, bleeding risk, life expectancy, anatomy, and patient values.
